subject: Application - (Senior) Platform Engineer, STACKIT Control Plane Platform (GT1923)
paragraphs: I am applying for the (Senior) Platform Engineer role on the STACKIT Control Plane Platform. A control plane is the part of a cloud that has no downtime budget of its own: it provisions the infrastructure everything else runs on, and its monitoring is only worth what it catches. I have spent four years building that layer for a small production estate rather than consuming one, which is why the posting reads to me as a description of work I already do at a smaller scale.

Provisioning as a function of a declared input, not a sequence of commands, is the core of my current setup. One flake declares thirteen NixOS hosts, each registered as a feature list, with the option surface derived rather than copied; a host is added by describing it and running the gate, and the same module check runs in CI and on the machines. That is not the Kubernetes operator pattern, and I will not claim it is, but the reconcile loop, the drift question and the habit of making the declaration the only place a decision lives are the same ones. Go is the language I write services in: bountystash is a single-binary Go service with append-only events, content-addressed specifications and both a terminal UI and HTTP endpoints, built and operated by me end to end.

The monitoring paragraph is the one I care most about, because the failure mode I design against is an alert nobody believes. A sentinel writes job status, generation age, disk pressure and pressure-stall figures every fifteen minutes; gatus pages on any state that is not ok; and a green socket is explicitly not treated as a finished job, because the ledger is what settles it. Alerting derived from recorded state, with the query kept next to the alert, is my default, and it is a smaller version of the availability and performance ownership your team carries for the platform's own products.

On the security side, the posting asks for contribution to best practices and compliance rather than a checklist, which matches how the estate is built: secrets encrypted per host with SOPS and age, SSH access only through a certificate authority with short-lived certificates, default-deny nftables, and patching ordered by the CISA KEV catalogue and exposure rather than by severity labels. Vulnerability work here produces a patch order and an exposure table, not a report.

The gaps are specific and worth naming before an interview. I have not operated Kubernetes clusters in production: my knowledge of its architecture, controllers and reconciliation model is real, but it comes from building an equivalent layer and from reading, not from running clusters with tenants on them. Helm, Kustomize, Terraform, Pulumi, Istio, Calico, Concourse and Flux are all absent from my tool history, because Nix and a task interface occupy those roles in my estate, and I would be learning the tooling rather than the concepts. On location, I am in south-west Germany, some 230 km from Bad Friedrichshall and roughly two and a half hours by car, so I would like to understand the expected on-site cadence before we go further; I am happy to travel for onboarding and for team weeks. I am a US citizen with German permanent residence and do not need sponsorship.
